During the development of the ACCESS Next Generation platform at **JP Morgan Chase**, several challenges emerged. The project involved consolidating multiple regional and legacy payment systems into a single global portal, which was a complex task given the disparate data models, client configurations, and compliance records across these systems. This required meticulous data migration efforts to ensure that all legacy data was accurately transferred into the new platform without disrupting live payment operations.

Additionally, the project faced high-stakes and high-pressure conditions due to aggressive Wall Street delivery timelines. The team had to maintain constant velocity across a complex, multi-workstream program. There were also jurisdiction-specific compliance challenges, as the platform needed to adhere to a patchwork of conflicting regulatory requirements across APAC, EMEA, and the Americas. This required a careful mapping of regulatory requirements into platform configuration constraints and designing a regional data visibility framework.

Moreover, the legacy user entitlement management system was cumbersome, requiring days of manual configuration per user. This was overhauled to introduce a more efficient role-based access control (RBAC) system, which reduced entitlement management from days to minutes.

Despite these challenges, Matt and his team successfully launched the ACCESS platform in April 2011, transforming JP Morgan's global payment operations into a unified digital experience for over **135,000** clients across **180+** countries.

The client raised concerns about rising defects, which caught Matt off guard since the metrics seemed strong. The issue stemmed from an engineer who was interpreting backlog stories on his own, writing tests after code completion, which made the coverage appear complete but allowed defects to slip through. The backlog itself was vague, lacking defined scenarios or a clear definition of done, which contributed to the problem.

Matt took ownership of the situation in front of the client and **Accenture** leadership, choosing to dig into the root causes rather than defending the metrics. He conducted a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite, openly showing the gaps. He then rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought in TDD experts to coach the team. Through hands-on coaching and restructuring agile rituals, the team learned to align better and improve their practices.

The result was a reduction in defect rates as the story quality and test-first discipline took hold. The client stopped finding defects that the dashboards couldn't see, restoring confidence. This experience reinforced for Matt that metrics mean nothing without the practice behind them, and cultural transformation requires consistent coaching, not just process change.

He recovered a Q4 release that was **3 weeks** behind, avoiding **$500K** in penalties, and the program was delivered **3%** under budget with zero critical defects at launch.

Want to hear how he moved that team from 6-month waterfall releases to 2-week sprints?

🐾 Here's a great example.

At **Fiserv**, Matt transformed the team from a traditional waterfall approach with 6-month release cycles to agile methodologies with 2-week sprints. This lack of transparency led to multiple missed deadlines and client stakeholders threatening contract cancellation.

To ensure continuous collaboration and feedback, he introduced bi-weekly sprint demos that forced early sign-off on branding, UI, and ADA compliance. This approach allowed the team to catch issues early instead of discovering them six months into the process.

Within just three months, Matt successfully transitioned the team to a 2-week sprint cadence. This change provided real-time visibility to over **50 stakeholders** across three time zones, replacing static steering committee reporting. The agile transformation not only satisfied PMO and compliance audit requirements but also empowered offshore teams to adopt an empowerment model, integrating screen reader audits into their Definition of Done.
